title: 🚀 [Classification Blueprint] GPU Target Encoding + XGBoost + Probe Feature Selection Body UNDER 5 MINUTES
content:
Hey everyone!

I wanted to share a highly optimized, end-to-end classification blueprint I built for this Phone Addiction dataset. If you are struggling with high cardinality, memory crashes, or slow training times, this pipeline is designed to bypass all of those bottlenecks using pure GPU acceleration.

Notebook Link: Phone Addiction Model - GPU Blueprint

Here is a breakdown of the techniques used in this notebook:

1. 100% GPU-Accelerated Pipeline (RAPIDS)

  • Uses cudf for blazing-fast data manipulation and cuml for Target Encoding. The data stays on the GPU, drastically reducing training time.

2. Leak-Proof Target Encoding (Inside the CV Loop)

  • To prevent data leakage, the CuMLTargetEncoder is applied strictly inside the Stratified K-Fold loop.
  • Test-Time Augmentation (TTA): The test set is encoded 5 different times based on the 5 training folds, and the final predictions are averaged for maximum stability.

3. Automated Feature Engineering

  • Categorical Interactions: Brute-force string concatenations for all categorical pairs.
  • Domain Math: Custom numerical ratios (e.g., screen_to_sleep_ratio) to feed XGBoost the exact behavioral metrics it struggles to calculate on its own.

4. The "Probe Model" (Noise Reduction)

  • Before feeding 200+ features into XGBoost, a blazing-fast LightGBM "Probe" model ranks the features by importance.
  • It ruthlessly drops the bottom 5% of features (pure noise), saving memory and preventing the tree models from overfitting on useless interactions.

5. Optuna-Tuned XGBoost Champion

  • The final model is a heavily regularized XGBoost classifier (tree_method='hist', device='cuda') tuned specifically to maximize ROC AUC.

I would love to hear your thoughts, feedback, or any suggestions on how to improve the feature engineering further!

If you find the blueprint useful for your own models, an upvote is highly appreciated! Happy Kaggling! 🏆

title: 🚀 Breaking the 0.97100 Wall (Highest Public Notebook) & The Art of LB Probing
content:
Hi everyone! 👋

If you look at the Leaderboard distribution, there is a massive spike right at 0.97099 and 0.97100. It seems a huge portion of the community is stuck hitting this exact ceiling using the available public blends.

While my main models are currently cooking on the GPU with proper OOF validation, I didn’t want my daily submission slots to go to waste. So, I decided to do a fun, educational experiment: What does it actually take to mathematically force a score of 0.97101?

I just published a notebook documenting this journey:

👉 https://www.kaggle.com/code/najiama/ensemble-of-ensembles-lb-0-97101

🎯 Notebook Objective

The goal was to take Rayk Kretzschmar's excellent 0.97100 baseline and inject my own high-scoring LGBM (OOF 0.9687) and a highly diverse KNN model to break the tie.

I logged all the failed experiments (Logit blending, uncertainty masking, etc.) which all dropped the score or stayed flat. Finally, I managed to squeeze out the +0.00001 to reach 0.97101 using an advanced (and slightly dangerous) technique called Reverse Micro-Sorting.

By dividing the predictions into 500 buckets and reversing my LGBM's predictions inside those tight clusters, it corrected the LB bias and gave us the bump!

📊 Leaderboard Context

As of today (Aug 15, 2026), this makes it the highest-scoring public notebook by +0.00001. However, as you can see in the histogram I attached, hitting 0.97101 only puts us at #39 on the LB! The absolute top competitors (#1) are sitting way out at 0.97124, proving there is still genuine ML signal to be found beyond just blending public scripts.

🛑 Disclaimer & Thoughts

I made this notebook public because it is a perfect, live demonstration of Public LB Overfitting. By mathematically reversing a strong model just to gain 0.00001 on 20% of the data, this submission is almost guaranteed to sink like a stone in the Private LB shakeup. 😅

I'd love to hear your thoughts and comments!

  • Have you managed to break past 0.97100 using honest CV without overfitting?
  • How brutal do we think the shakeup will be for the 0.97100 cluster?

Check out the notebook, and if you find the experiment helpful (or at least entertaining), I’d appreciate an upvote! Good luck to everyone working on their final models! 🚀

title: Model capacity was worth 18x my feature engineering — and then made it worthless
content:
I built 15 engineered features for this competition and got +0.0004 AUC. Then I changednum_leaves` from 15 to 31 and got +0.0077.

Then I re-ran the feature ablation at the corrected capacity, and the features stopped helping entirely:

CV AUC delta
base, num_leaves=15 0.95132 —
+ 15 features, num_leaves=15 0.95175 +0.00042
base, num_leaves=31 0.95905 +0.00773
+ 15 features, num_leaves=31 0.95859 −0.00046

(200k subsample, 3-fold, 2 seeds, paired seed-by-seed deltas. On the full 691k with 5 folds and 3 seeds, base and +eng both land on exactly 0.9637.)

My reading: almost every feature I built was a ratio or difference of existing columns, and a tree with enough leaves constructs those itself. The +0.0004 was never the value of the features — it was the cost of the underfitting they were papering over. My defaults came from an 891-row problem and I never revisited them.

Full ablation, runnable end to end: https://www.kaggle.com/code/wowtimwow/model-capacity-beat-my-feature-engineering-by-18x

One thing I have not tested: gender, stress_level and academic_work_impact have ~0 mutual information globally, but all the remaining error is concentrated in the 5–8.7h screen-time band. Does anyone know whether they carry signal conditionally inside that band?`

column AUC, all rows AUC, 5–8.7h band
gender 0.5119 0.5132

academic_work_impact 0.5019 0.5036

This looks like feature utility being conditional on effective tree capacity, but the 15-to-31-leaf change is still only one slice through the capacity surface. A useful falsifier would sweep num_leaves × min_data_in_leaf on identical folds and seeds, record the early-stopped iteration count, and plot the paired engineered-minus-base AUC against realized tree capacity. If the sign changes only under one regularization setting, it may instead be an optimization interaction. For the 5–8.7h band, I would test conditional value through held-out model residuals rather than target-encoding AUC.

The goal is not only to analyze this particular dataset, but to create a structured EDA workflow that can be adapted to similar classification problems involving mixed numerical and categorical features.

  • Numerical and categorical feature identification
  • Target variable distribution
  • Class imbalance analysis
  • Univariate analysis
  • Numerical feature distributions
  • Mean, median and distribution analysis
  • Outlier analysis
  • Categorical feature frequency analysis
  • Rare-category detection using frequency thresholds
  • Bivariate analysis
  • Feature relationships with the target
  • Correlation analysis
  • Distribution comparisons across target classes
  • Visualizations designed for quick pattern identification

🎯 Objective

The main objective of this blueprint is to make the EDA process systematic, reusable and competition-ready rather than performing isolated visualizations for individual datasets. It can serve as a starting point for quickly understanding a new dataset, identifying data-quality issues, discovering useful patterns and generating hypotheses before moving into feature engineering and model development.

🚀 Why a Blueprint?

Instead of rebuilding an EDA workflow from scratch for every competition, this notebook organizes commonly required analysis into a reusable structure. The blueprint can be extended with additional statistical tests, feature engineering techniques and model-specific diagnostics depending on the dataset and competition objective.

title: 📱 S6E8 | Boosting AUC with Rank Transformation & Missing Value Indicators
content:
Hi everyone,

I've been experimenting with feature engineering for the Addiction Prediction competition. Here are two techniques that provided a solid boost to my local OOF AUC:

  1. Rank Transformation: Continuous features like daily_screen_time_hours and app_opens_per_day have significant outliers. Converting these to percentile ranks (df[col].rank(pct=True)) helps models like LightGBM and XGBoost handle the scale better.
  2. Missing Value Indicators: Every single feature in this dataset has missing values. Instead of just imputing, adding binary flags for nulls (df[col].isnull()) allows the model to learn if the "missingness" itself is predictive.

I've shared a notebook implementing these here: https://www.kaggle.com/code/dynamo14324/s6e8-advanced-feature-engineering

What other interaction features are you finding useful?

title: How are you designing Private-LB-robust validation for S6E8?
content:
Hi everyone,

I’m exploring validation strategies for S6E8, especially approaches that are robust to the Private leaderboard rather than narrowly optimized for the Public split.

A few observations and questions:

  1. Standard stratified CV appears useful, but small leaderboard differences may not be reliable. Have you found grouped, ID-block, missingness-stratified, or adversarial validation more predictive of leaderboard stability?

  2. Tree models and tabular deep models seem complementary. In my experiments, LightGBM/CatBoost, value-embedding or transformer-style models, and RealMLP-like models make somewhat different errors. Have you found rank averaging more stable than probability blending or stacking?

  3. For cross-model distillation, there is a subtle leakage risk: ordinary teacher OOF predictions are not necessarily safe as training targets inside a different student outer fold, because some teacher models may have seen the student validation labels. I currently avoid this using nested teacher OOF predictions generated only inside each student outer-training fold. Has anyone tested similar leakage-safe distillation here?

  4. Missing-value patterns appear important. Do you model missingness only as indicators, or treat missing patterns/combinations as categorical features?

  5. Has anyone found a reliable way to use the original 7,500-row dataset? Exact train/test feature overlap seems extremely limited, while direct target transfer from the original data does not validate particularly well for me.

  6. For Public/Private robustness, what diagnostics have been most useful besides overall OOF AUC—for example fold variance, contiguous ID-block scores, missingness buckets, or model-disagreement slices?

I’m mainly interested in reproducible methodology and Private-LB robustness, not Public-LB probing or leaderboard leakage.

Thanks—interested to hear what validation evidence has held up best for others.

messages.text:
Six questions, and I can put measurements on four. Here they are in your order, with the two I cannot answer marked as such.

Grouped, ID-block, missingness-stratified or adversarial splits. I have not run them head to head, so I cannot rank them. What made me stop looking for a cleverer split is Dariush Afshar's adversarial run: train against test scores 0.564 on raw features, 0.503 once missingness is imputed away, and 0.498 on complete rows only. His own caveat matters for your question specifically, because the last row is a statement about the complete-row subpopulation: if drift lived only in the observed values of incomplete rows, that design would not see it. Taking it at face value, there is no value drift for a drift-aware split to correct, only missingness.

Rank averaging against probability blending against stacking. Measured on szymonkapiski's 74-member library, one frozen five-fold split, four corners of the same square:

equal weights hill-climbed
best ten members 0.96931 0.96942
all seventy-four 0.96738 0.96948

The two choices interact, which is the part I would take away. Under equal weights the member list is worth +0.00193 and the weights +0.00011. Under hill climbing the member list is worth -0.00006 and the weights +0.00210. Averaging punishes a bad pool and fitting rescues it, so "prune first" and "fit weights" are answers to the same question rather than two independent gains. A nested logistic stack over all seventy-four beats every cell at 0.96963, because it can hand a member a negative weight and use a weak model as a correction, which hill climbing cannot: that is szymonkapiski's own design and his own explanation of the negative weights.

I blend on ranks rather than probabilities, but that is a decision, not a measurement. AUC is rank-only and the members are not calibrated to a common scale, so averaging probabilities averages their calibrations too.

Leakage-safe distillation. Not measured, and I will not guess. Your objection reads as correct to me and nested teacher OOF inside each student outer fold is the conservative construction. If you measure the difference it deserves its own thread.

Missingness as indicators or as pattern categoricals. Neither pays as a standalone. The count of missing columns ranks at 0.502 on its own, and the largest gap any single column opens between its missing and present rows is 0.0042 against a base rate of 0.709. Dariush measured the flags on the target task at -0.000002 for the nine numeric ones and -0.000045 for the three categorical.

One caveat I owe, since I am currently in the middle of it: my own gate bundles a count of observed components together with tamerlanomralinov's budget-slack column, and that bundle does clear the gate. I never ran the two apart, so I cannot tell you which one carries it, and "the count is worth nothing" is a claim my own table does not support yet.

And a distinction that keeps catching people here, me included. Missingness carries nothing about the target and a great deal about which split a row came from: Dariush's flags-only adversarial AUC is 0.565. Both true, different questions, and a sentence that does not say which one it means gets read as the other.

The 7,500-row table. Read it, do not train on it. tomasa2 measured concatenating it at -0.00008 against his own pipeline. I would also not call it the original: it is a candidate mirror, two independent uploads of it are byte-identical so they share an ancestor, and that is all anyone has shown. What it is good for is that the label rule is legible in it and smoothed in ours. broccoli beef found the rule and Busya PRIME measured the smoothing. Separately from the rule, the largest single lever on this data is encoding each column by its exact value rather than its magnitude, which picks up the generator's rounding lattice: OMID BAGHCHEH SARAEI's idea, measured independently by tomasa2, shipped by tamerlanomralinov.

Diagnostics beyond OOF AUC. This is the one that matters, and I would put a resolution floor first. szymonkapiski published the arithmetic in his honest OOF blend on 4 August, bootstrapping to the full test size of 296,302 rows: the standard deviation of a single AUC is 0.000272, of a difference between two correlated submissions 0.000072, and the multiplier is sqrt(2(1-rho)). He notes it measures row-sampling noise only, not the public-private split, and the public half is a quarter of the test, so the same arithmetic is roughly twice as loose there.

What Dariush added, and what I had missing until he pointed it out in his thread, is that the answer splits on correlation rather than being one number. What I measured on top of that is how far it moves: across seven pairs built from that library, the smallest resolvable difference runs from 0.000005 for two near-identical blends to 0.00043 for one single model against another. So "is my gain above the floor" has no answer until you say whose floor, and the floor between your own two final candidates is much lower than the floor between you and a stranger.

For the private half I joined the seven finished Season 6 boards into a dataset and worked through them here. Three of the seven erased their public top ten, four kept five or more, none landed in between. The part that went against me is that I could not build a ruler to tell those two groups apart in advance: the one I liked stopped separating them once I cut the finished boards down to the size this board is at now, and the one that survives that cut survives it by construction rather than by test. title: The Generator Didn't Just Smooth the Labels — It Fixed the Data
content:
We checked internal consistency across the original 7,500-row survey and the 691K synthetic competition data. The original has widespread arithmetic violations; the generator cleaned them all up.

Original data: 26% of respondents report social + gaming > total screen time.

Constraint Generated Original
social_media + gaming > screen_time 0% 26.3%
social_media > screen_time 0% 9.1%
work_study > screen_time 0% 9.1%
gaming > screen_time 0% 1.5%

The mean of entertainment_ratio = (social + gaming) / screen_time drops from 0.815 (Original) to 0.524 (Generated). Gen Train and Gen Test are identical to 3 decimal places.

Why this matters:

  1. Generator learned sum(parts) ≤ whole and enforces it perfectly — the generator didn't just soften hard rules into probabilities, it repaired the feature space.

  2. This creates a clean distribution shift: ratio-based features are safe on the competition data (0% violations) but would break on real-world survey data.

Combined with [the finding that the generator turned a 2-rule lookup table into a smooth probability field], this paints a consistent picture: the generator is the signal. It manufactured learnable structure where the original had noise (the "otherwise" region goes from AUC 0.50 → 0.90), reshaped every marginal into smooth monotone curves, and enforced physical constraints that the real survey didn't.

title: Decoding the Synthetic Generator: 0.9689+ via Stringified Target Encoding and Rank Averaging
content:
Hello everyone,

During my exploratory data analysis (EDA) of the synthetic dataset in Playground Series S6E8, I observed that treating the continuous variables as standard floating-point numericals yields suboptimal results for tree-based models. I would like to share a highly effective methodology that improved my Public LB to 0.9689+: transforming all continuous numerical variables into categorical strings prior to applying Target (Mean) Encoding.

Here is a detailed breakdown of the insights and the modeling pipeline:

1 - Exploiting the Synthetic Nature: Exact Mapping vs. Continuous Splitting

The training data is generated synthetically, and we must explicitly adapt to its generation mechanics. A close examination of features such as sleep_hours, notifications_per_day, and app_opens_per_day reveals highly jagged, discrete grid patterns rather than smooth continuous distributions.

Crucially, the distributions in the synthetic training set almost perfectly overlap with the original, much smaller dataset. This indicates that the generator did not learn an underlying mathematical distribution but rather forcefully replicated the exact mappings and discrete artifacts of the source data. Consequently, asking tree models to search for logical continuous splits is inherently inefficient. By switching to a rigorous lookup-table approach, we compel the model to memorize these exact empirical probabilities, effectively reverse-engineering the data generator.

2 - The Methodology: Stringified Target Encoding

Instead of utilizing raw continuous features, I applied .astype(str) to all continuous variables, thereby treating each unique floating-point value as a distinct categorical class.

Following this discretization, I applied Target Encoding (Mean Encoding). This transforms the categorical strings into robust probability metrics. Mathematically, this acts as a high-dimensional mapping dictionary, performing significant dimensionality reduction. The tree models are no longer required to make thousands of microscopic splits; they simply follow the mapped probability values.

3 - Statistical Robustness via 10-Fold OOF Encoding

To strictly prevent data leakage and ensure the lookup tables are extremely accurate, the Target Encoding was computed within a 10-Fold Stratified K-Fold cross-validation framework.

Using 10 folds instead of 5 ensures that 90% of the dataset is utilized to calculate the out-of-fold (OOF) target probabilities. For highly sparse grid points at the tails of the distribution, a larger statistical base is critical for accurately estimating the generator's true underlying probability logic.

4 - Ensemble Strategy: Rank Averaging

When blending the predictions from LightGBM and XGBoost (GPU), gradient-based optimization algorithms (like SLSQP) and simple arithmetic averaging failed to yield improvements. This occurs because the absolute probability scales and confidence intervals of the two models differ significantly.

The Solution: Using scipy.stats.rankdata. By converting the absolute predicted probabilities into relative ranks and averaging those ranks, we perfectly align the predictions and neutralize any extreme scale discrepancies, resulting in a highly stable final AUC score.

I have open-sourced the complete, clean code in my notebook here: https://www.kaggle.com/code/echloeprice/phone-addiction-prediction . If you want to more about how I iterated toward it, check this one: https://www.kaggle.com/code/echloeprice/phone-addict

title: Changing the random seed moves you 60 places — what this leaderboard can and can't resolve
content:
The gap between rank 1 and rank 50 is 0.00031 AUC, which invites the conclusion that the ordering is noise. The obvious way to check that — the standard error of an AUC estimate — gives the wrong answer, and it is worth being precise about why.

Hanley–McNeil says SE ≈ 0.00066 for AUC 0.971 on ~59,000 rows, which would put 112 teams inside one sigma of first place. But nobody compares their score to the truth; everyone is scored on the same rows. Shared shocks cancel in the difference and not in either score. Measured over 300 LB-sized resamples, the paired sigma is 0.00009–0.00011 — six to seven times smaller.

Three consequences:

The board resolves more than it looks like. #1 vs #50 is ~3 sigma. Real. The very top does not. #1 vs #2 is ~1 sigma, and two seeds of the same model swap places about half the time. Rank is much noisier than score. Between rank 10 and rank 100 the board is packed tightly enough that ±1 sigma of pure reseed noise spans ~60 teams. Practical rule that falls out: if a change moves you 40 places but moves your score by less than 0.0001, you have measured nothing.

title: A quarter of the rows describe people who can't exist — and LightGBM already knew
content:
In the source dataset, weekend_screen_time is not an independent column: it is weekday screen time times a factor, and that factor never leaves [1.044, 1.965] across all 7,500 original rows.

The generator did not learn that. 26% of competition rows fall outside the envelope, in train and test alike (73.8% / 73.9% inside — so nothing exploitable as leakage). Those rows behave completely differently: inside the plausible band the target fires 81% of the time, past 2.5× it fires 25%, against a 71% base rate. Neither parent column shows it, because the relationship is a hump and both columns are monotone.

Then I measured it instead of just telling the story: handing the ratio to LightGBM is worth −0.00007 AUC, against a seed-to-seed spread of ±0.00004. The trees were already carving out the region on their own.

So it is a null result, and the interesting part is what survives it: anything monotone — a logistic regression, a rank-average blend, a monotone-constrained booster — structurally cannot represent this, which tells you where a linear component in your ensemble is losing.

Also in there: missingness is MCAR (n_missing scores AUC 0.502), so null-indicator features are 12 columns of noise.

content:
Map Choice Prediction Challenge

In many multiplayer online games, players vote on which map to play before a match begins, and the game system selects a final map based on all players' choices. This competition provides a large dataset of game sessions from a fictional online game, where each session records 8 players' map selections (from 16 available maps, numbered 0–15) along with the timestamps of their votes, as well as the timestamp of the voting window. Your task is to predict the final map selected by the system for each session. The dataset is synthetically generated with realistic game mechanics, and the evaluation metric is Accuracy.

this competition, you are tasked with predicting which map a game system will ultimately select for a match, based on the voting behavior of 8 players. Each player chooses from 16 available maps (numbered 0 to 15), and each vote is accompanied by a precise timestamp. The dataset includes the timestamp of when the voting window opened, the timestamp of each player's vote, and each player's map choice.

Your objective is to build a model that learns the mapping from these inputs to the system's final selection. The training data contains the ground-truth target labels, while the test data does not. This is a classification task with 16 possible classes, evaluated using Accuracy.

The data is synthetically generated and designed to be both realistic and challenging. Success in this competition requires careful feature engineering, particularly around the temporal and ordering aspects of the data. Good luck! 🎮

Your finding is real, and there is something stranger sitting underneath it.

First, the bend. It moves. Hold social media inside a narrow band and count the addicted share by daily screen time on train.csv, and the point where it crosses one half slides a long way:

social media addicted share, daily 2h through 11h
0 to 1h 0.11 0.03 0.03 0.08 0.24 0.47 0.78 0.97 1.00
1 to 2h 0.47 0.43 0.31 0.25 0.35 0.57 0.82 0.98 1.00
2 to 3h 0.69 0.64 0.66 0.70 0.78 0.88 0.98 1.00 1.00

Read the first two rows left to right. The share goes down before it goes up. At one hour of social media, someone on four hours of screen time is less likely to be addicted than someone on two. Your line at six hours is what those rows look like once they are averaged together, so it is real in the aggregate and it is not one boundary sitting in one place.

That dip is worth more attention than the bend, because nothing about the domain predicts it and it is not noise: it shows up in three of the four social bands wide enough to count, and in all three the Wilson intervals at the peak and at the trough do not overlap. The fourth band, social above three hours, has no dip at all, which is its own clue. broccoli beef and Busya PRIME have both dug into how these rows were generated, in Generation model of the missing "original" dataset and The generator turned a hard rule into a smooth field, and they are the right places to read next.

Which brings me to the part you asked about.

The likely reason nothing you built moved the score is the shape of what you built. If it was a flag or a threshold on daily and social, the model can already reach it: those are two columns it splits on directly, and it can cut that corner itself in as many steps as it needs. Handing a tree a boundary it can already draw buys nothing.

What a tree cannot do in one split is arithmetic across columns. The boundary here is tilted rather than square: inside the region below six hours of screen time and four of social, the addicted share runs from 0.027 to 0.794, and almost all of that movement comes from social rather than daily. A tilted boundary costs a tree a staircase of splits, and a single column that already holds the sum or the difference saves it. That is the class of feature that pays here, and it is a different class from the one you tried.

The measurements, all on one reference model, five folds, out of fold, one feature at a time:

feature worth
slack and a count of observed components, tamerlanomralinov's +0.00071
daily - (social + gaming + work), Dariush Afshar's, built on ryota517's budget constraint +0.00058
a one-sided bound for when social is missing, mine +0.00024
a placebo column: random values, same missingness pattern -0.00002

Every real one is positive on all five folds; the placebo is positive on three, which is what nothing looks like. That placebo is the part I would copy first. It costs one column and it tells you whether your +0.0003 is a feature or a fold.

Two things are worth more than any of them, and unlike the rows above these two stack rather than being added one at a time. Going from 63 leaves and 400 rounds to 255 and 1500 with a smaller learning rate was worth +0.0012. Target-encoding each column by its exact value, rather than treating it as a magnitude, was worth +0.0032 on top of that. The encoding is OMID BAGHCHEH SARAEI's idea, measured independently by tomasa2 and shipped by tamerlanomralinov. If you try it, fit the encoding inside each training fold and never on the full training set, or your validation score will jump by a lot and none of it will be real.

On your last question I have to be straight: every number above is LightGBM, and I have not run XGBoost at all, so I cannot tell you which library is better. title: 5 Features, Logistic Regression, ~0.945 ROC AUC
content:
Hello colleagues!

I'd like to share some research I've been conducting over the past few days, I'm interested in your thoughts or criticism. The result is a logistic regression trained on five original features that reaches a decent ROC AUC. It obviously can't compete with a tuned CatBoost or an ensemble, but in a competition like this I'm always more interested in finding the simplest and interpretable models :) Here I'll tell how I came this result.

I dropped all rows with missing values for this analysis. I plan to revisit this with imputation and see whether it changes anything.

Step 1: Bayesian networks

I started by building Bayesian networks by hand and checking how well different edge sets described the data. I also ran structure-learning algorithms (pgmpy, Hill-Climb search with a few scoring functions). Both approaches converged to the same picture: simple structure where the target is connected to only 2-3 variables. Manually-built, more complex networks were not really better than simple structure based on likelihood.

Step 2: Conditional Mutual Information

To get a cleaner, non-graph-based confirmation, I computed I(X; target | Z) for every pair of features X, Z, and also for pairs of conditioning variables I(X; target | Z1, Z2). The logic: if conditioning on some Z drives the CMI to ~0, X likely has no direct edge to the target - its influence is mediated through Z.

This showed:

  • daily_screen_time_hours and weekend_screen_time are highly redundant with each other - their mutual dependence stays large even after conditioning on the target.
  • social_media_hours keeps a small residual link to the target even after conditioning on the screen-time pair.
  • gaming_hours, work_study_hours, app_opens_per_day become almost uninformative once conditioned on the screen-time variables.
  • academic_work_impact, stress_level, gender, age, sleep_hours, notifications_per_day stay near-zero CMI under every conditioning set I tried - consistent with noise rather than signal.

Step 3: which features actually matter - decision trees + permutation importance

To validate the CMI picture with a completely different method, I ran a systematic search: decision trees at depths 1-10, over several nested feature subsets (single features, the screen-time pair, +social_media, +gaming/work_study, all 12 features, and a "noise cluster" of the suspected-irrelevant variables), scored with 5-fold CV accuracy/AUC.

Key findings:

  • The 3-feature set (daily_screen_time_hours, social_media_hours, weekend_screen_time) almost matches the CV accuracy/AUC of the full 12-feature set.
  • CV accuracy peaks at tree depth 2 and doesn't improve further; CV AUC keeps improving up to depth ~8, which is a signature of an underlying smooth probabilistic relationship rather than a hard threshold rule.
  • The noise cluster of features (stress/academic/gender/age/sleep) gets AUC ≈ 0.52-0.58 on its own.
  • I also bootstrapped depth-1 trees (30 resamples) to see which feature wins the root split most consistently: daily_screen_time_hours won 30/30 times, with an almost identical threshold each time (std ≈ 0.007).
  • Permutation importance from a Random Forest on all 12 features ranked social_media_hours slightly above daily_screen_time_hours and weekend_screen_time - different from the single-tree ranking, but expected given that these features are highly correlated.
  • gaming_hours/work_study_hours showed a small but consistently non-zero contribution; gender/stress_level/academic_work_impact were essentially at zero.

Step 4: how close can a logistic regression get

With the 3 key features, I compared logistic regression variants against GradientBoosting/RandomForest trained on the same 3 features (as a ceiling estimate of how much signal is even extractable from them):

  • Plain linear logistic regression: AUC ≈ 0.927 - clearly below the ceiling (≈0.951 GBM / ≈0.943 RF), so the true relationship isn't linear in log-odds.
  • Degree-2 polynomial logistic regression (squares + pairwise interactions): AUC ≈ 0.943 - essentially matches the RF ceiling.
  • I've also tested some other variants but they were not so impressive.

Step 5: gaming_hours / work_study_hours

I tested this with a likelihood-ratio test comparing logistic regression on the 3 core features vs. core+these 2 extra features. The improvement was statistically significant, so the effect is real. But the effect size is small, and inside the "ambiguous zone" (predictions near 0.5 from the core model) the two extra features together only reach AUC ≈ 0.58. Looking at mean residuals across bins of each variable, the shape isn't monotonic - closer to a wave than a straight line, which a single linear coefficient doesn't fully capture.

Final model

Based on all of this, the final logistic regression uses 5 features (daily_screen_time_hours, social_media_hours, weekend_screen_time, gaming_hours, work_study_hours) with all squares and pairwise interactions included. This reached ROC AUC close to what Random Forest achieves on the same features (~0.945-0.95). CatBoost achieved an ROC AUC of approximately 0.96 on both the full feature set and a subset reduced to the top 5 features in this dataset.

I've also conducted some further analysis of the resulting logit function for fun :) I looked at the resulting logit as a quadratic function and found its stationary point (numbers are written in next order: "daily_screen_time_hours", "social_media_hours", "weekend_screen_time", "gaming_hours", "work_study_hours"):

(3.362, 6.982, 0.016, 2.628, 2.669)

Hessian eigenvalues: 

22.868, 2.061, −0.373, −1.799, −2.869

with corresponding eigenvectors:

v1 ≈ (−0.879, 0.372, −0.299, −0.014, −0.011)
v2 ≈ (0.275, −0.107, −0.948, 0.038, 0.111)
v3 ≈ (0.328, 0.833, 0.049, 0.335, 0.290)
v4 ≈ (0.074, 0.170, 0.018, −0.879, 0.439)
v5 ≈ (−0.199, −0.357, 0.094, 0.337, 0.843)

Mixed signs among the eigenvalues mean this stationary point is a saddle, and there are two directions along which the logit increases and three along which it decreases. The model is a curved surface where the outcome depends on how features move together.

I still need to figure out where this model goes wrong, but I've already used it to extract certain data properties, which I'll describe later.

Later, I'll also add some visualizations I've created and deeper analysis of resulting model.

For now you can observe some **code ** made here: https://www.kaggle.com/code/vladstud716373618/5-features-logistic-regression-0-945-roc-auc.

Thank you for your attention! :)

title: 27 teams show 0.97086. None of them are tied.
content:
(All leaderboard numbers below are from one snapshot: the public LB as of 2026-08-07 06:06 UTC, 942 teams. Pinned so you can reproduce them — the board moves fast.)

Right now 27 teams display exactly 0.97086 on the public leaderboard, spread across ranks 19–45. That looks like a plateau you need a full +0.00001 to escape.

It isn't a plateau, and you don't.

Kaggle ranks on the full-precision score. The five decimals are display rounding. Those 27 teams are ordered internally at a precision the leaderboard never shows you.

How to check it from the leaderboard file alone

If ranking used the rounded score with a submission-date tie-break, then inside every displayed-score group rank would be perfectly date-ordered — spearman(rank, date) = +1.000, every group. Measured on the 2026-08-07 board (942 teams), all 11 groups with n ≥ 5:

displayed score n spearman(rank, LastSubmissionDate)
0.97086 27 +0.363
0.97084 21 −0.396
0.97068 10 −0.091
0.97083 7 −0.357
0.96374 5 −0.800
0.50000 6 +1.000
mean over all 11 groups +0.106

Exactly one group is perfectly date-ordered: the six teams at 0.50000, every one of them a single-submission team, sitting at ranks 935–940 in exact date order. Those scores really are identical (AUC 0.5), so Kaggle falls back to a date tie-break and the signature shows up clean. It shows up nowhere else. No other visible column explains the within-group order either — averaged over groups, spearman(rank, SubmissionCount) = +0.010 and spearman(rank, TeamId) = +0.038.

Closing the obvious objection

That control doesn't finish the job, because Kaggle could rank on the rounded score and break ties by the date each team first achieved it — which the leaderboard file doesn't expose. Every team in the 0.50000 group has one submission, so that group can't separate the two explanations.

Here's the test that can. A team whose entire submission history ended before you first reached a score necessarily reached their score before you reached yours. Under first-achieved tie-breaking, every one of them must rank ahead of you.

I first hit 0.97086 on 2026-08-07 at 00:01:39. In that group:

  • 20 teams' last submission of any kind predates that moment
  • 19 of them rank behind me
  • under rounded-score-plus-first-achieved, that number must be 0

One case makes it concrete: a team with exactly one submission, made 2026-08-06 05:48 — eighteen hours before I first reached the score — ranks 32 to my 21.

And a live check: I submitted again at 06:24, making me the newest submitter in the group. My rank didn't move (21 → 21). Under any last-submission tie-break I'd have dropped to ~45.

Three independent tests, one answer: the "ties" aren't ties.

What a rank actually costs

Model each displayed band as its teams spread across its 1e-05 width (your own rank pins where you sit inside yours). Near 0.97086:

  • ~1.6 ranks per 1e-06 of AUC
  • one rank costs ≈4e-07, not 1e-05
true AUC gain ranks gained new rank (from 21/942)
+1e-06 +2 19
+5e-06 +3 18
+1e-05 +4 17
+3e-05 +8 13
+1e-04 +15 6

The part that should worry you

This is not a licence to celebrate small gains. It cuts the other way.

Kaggle keeps your best public score, so a resubmission can only help your displayed rank, never hurt it. Combine that with a rank costing 4e-07 and you get an uncomfortable result: firing a near-duplicate with no real improvement at all is a coin flip you cannot lose.

I measured it on two of my own submissions correlated at ρ = 0.999897 — bootstrap the paired AUC difference 4,000× at public-split size (~59k rows), price each draw through the rank curve above, then repeat with the same draws re-centred to mean zero (same disagreement structure, no edge):

candidate E[ranks gained] P(rank improves)
real edge (+7.3e-06 CV, 5/5 folds, 15/15 across three fold partitions) 2.91 0.815
zero-edge twin 1.44 0.486

So a genuine edge was worth about +1.5 ranks over simply resubmitting. Half the apparent gain isn't skill — it's best-of-N.

And that half doesn't shrink with more data. Across public splits of 20% / 30% / 50%, the zero-edge twin's P(rank improves) is 0.486 / 0.480 / 0.458 — near-constant, because it's just the chance a zero-mean draw lands positive. A bigger public split makes your edge more resolvable; it does nothing about the free coin flip.

One side-finding I had wrong myself and think is genuinely useful: the sampling SD of the paired difference at 59k rows is 7.6e-06, roughly 10× tighter than you'd get comparing two unrelated models. Resolvability isn't a fixed threshold you can quote once — it scales with 1−ρ. Two near-twins are compared far more precisely than two different models are.

What I'd actually do with this

  1. Don't read a displayed tie as a plateau. You're being ranked more finely than you're being shown.
  2. Don't read your public rank as a measurement. Near the top it's substantially a max-of-N statistic over your own submission history. Discount it — including your own. I have 22 submissions and several are near-twins, so some of my rank 21 was bought this way rather than earned.
  3. Pick finals on cross-validation, not on this board. The private split is ~4× the public one, so a real CV edge is far likelier to survive there than a public-rank bump is to have been real in the first place.

An honest counter-observation, since it happened tonight: the +7.3e-06 candidate above is one I actually fired, and my rank did not move — 0 ranks where the curve predicted ~3. That's an 18.5% draw under the model. One public-split draw is much weaker evidence than 15/15 folds, so I'm not revising anything — but it's a fair warning that the price curve is not something you can reliably cash.

Everything above the bootstrap section is reproducible from the public leaderboard CSV alone. This is measured from the board's behaviour, not from Kaggle documentation — I'd genuinely like to see a case that breaks it.

title: I Injected Real-World Data Into My Model and Every Single Fold Got Worse
content:
I Injected Real-World Data Into My Model and Every Single Fold Got Worse. That Was the Best Thing That Happened All Competition.

Every synthetic tabular competition has the same rumor: somewhere out there is the "real" dataset the generator was trained on, and if you can find it, you've found free signal. I found it. 7,500 real rows, buried behind the competition's synthetic 691,369-row train set. I weighted them into training at 50x. Ten folds later, all ten had dropped below baseline.

Notebook link: https://www.kaggle.com/code/muhammadf4h33m/s06e08-original-data-lightgbm-0-96169

Here's what that consistent drop actually taught me — and why the obvious explanation is probably the wrong one.

The Setup

Kaggle's synthetic Playground competitions are built by training a generator (commonly CTGAN) on a small real-world dataset, then sampling hundreds of thousands of synthetic rows from it. The original dataset almost never ships with the competition — but it's often findable, because the underlying study or survey exists publicly.

In this case: 7,500 real rows, 0 missing values, a 70.77% positive rate — nearly identical to the synthetic train set's 70.94%. On paper, this looked like the single best feature source available: real human behavior, not generator noise.

The Experiment

I injected the 7,500 real rows into every training fold with a 50x sample weight, on the theory that forcing the trees to prioritize genuine behavioral relationships would generalize better than fitting synthetic quirks.

title: Feature Engineering: What Works, What Fails, and the Math Behind It
content:
Most people write feature engineering, glance at the leaderboard, and keep whatever moved the number. I wanted to know why a feature works before I trust it — so instead of stacking features and hoping, I built a strict 10-fold ablation harness, ran adversarial validation against the test set, and null-tested every feature against pure noise.

The result surprised me: the "smart" behavioral features I was proudest of were actively hurting the model. The features that won were the ones that had nothing to do with psychology at all — they were reverse-engineered flaws in the synthetic data generator itself.

Notebook link: https://www.kaggle.com/code/muhammadf4h33m/eda-fe-predicting-smartphone-addiction

1. The Ablation Study: Ratios Lose, Artifacts Win

Instead of dumping every engineered feature into one model and eyeballing the result, I added them cumulatively and measured the exact Out-Of-Fold (OOF) AUC delta at each step.

Step OOF AUC Delta
Baseline (raw features) 0.96394 —
+ Behavioral ratios 0.96371 -0.00023
+ Structural artifacts 0.96459 +0.00088
+ Complex behavioral math 0.96415 -0.00043

The takeaway: hand-crafted ratios like sleep_deficit and dopamine_ratio made the model worse. LightGBM and XGBoost already find these divisions and differences on their own through splits — manually pre-computing them just adds correlated columns that eat into the feature-sampling fraction without adding information the trees didn't already have access to.

The one real jump (+0.00088) came from structural artifacts — features that don't describe human behavior at all, but describe how the data was generated:

  • other_screen: the residual between daily_screen_time_hours and the sum of its components (social + gaming + work), which exposes rows where the generator's internal math doesn't add up.
  • _decimals: the string length of each time column's decimal portion, which captures floating-point rounding artifacts left behind by the generator.

These aren't behavioral insight. They're a map of the generator's blind spots — and the tree is happy to use it.

2. Adversarial Validation: Making Sure I Wasn't Repeating the Same Mistake

Earlier in the competition, several people (myself included) found that explicit missingness flags like missing_count raised local CV but tanked the Public LB. The reason: the generator injected missing values at different rates in train versus test, so a "missingness" feature was really just a proxy for which split the row came from — a textbook case of covariate shift.

Before trusting my new structural features, I checked whether they had the same problem. I trained a classifier to distinguish train rows from test rows (Train=0, Test=1) using every feature, including the new ones.

The adversarial AUC came out to 0.56441 — a mild shift exists somewhere in the data — but the importance table tells the real story: the shift is driven almost entirely by the original Kaggle columns, particularly app_opens_per_day and notifications_per_day. My new structural features (other_screen, the _decimals columns) didn't crack the top 10. They're statistically isolated from the train/test drift, which means they're safe to lean on without risking another missingness-flag situation.

3. The Null Importance Check

As a final sanity check, I ran a null importance test: shuffle the target into pure noise, retrain, and record what "importance" looks like when there's genuinely nothing to learn. Any real feature scoring close to that noise baseline is decoration, not signal.

The structural features cleared the noise bar by a wide margin:

  • daily_screen_time_hours_decimals: 11.68x higher gain than its noise baseline
  • other_screen_abs: 8.83x higher gain than its noise baseline

That's strong evidence the model isn't imagining a pattern — it's genuinely exploiting the arithmetic and floating-point fingerprints the generator leaves behind.

Conclusion

Stop stacking hand-built behavioral ratios on top of models that can already learn them natively — on this dataset, they measurably diluted the signal. Drop missingness flags; they're a covariate-shift trap disguised as a feature. And if you're working with a synthetic tabular dataset, spend your energy where the real edge is hiding: the generator's own arithmetic and rounding mistakes, not the fictional psychology it's dressed up in.

Methodology note: all deltas above come from a 10-fold stratified ablation harness with adversarial validation and null-importance checks run independently for each feature group — not a single lucky CV split.

title: As a Beginner, What's the First Thing You Check in a Tabular Competition?
content:
What's the First Thing You Check in a Tabular Competition?

This is my first time participating in a Kaggle competition, and I'm trying to build good habits instead of jumping straight into modeling.

My current workflow is:

  • Check the dataset shape and feature types.
  • Look for missing values and duplicates.
  • Understand the target distribution.
  • Train a simple baseline model before trying any tuning.

One thing I'm still unsure about is how experienced Kagglers decide where to spend their time first.

For example, when you open a new tabular competition:

  • Do you spend more time on EDA or start with a baseline immediately?
  • Which usually gives you the biggest leaderboard improvement: feature engineering, cross-validation, or hyperparameter tuning?
  • What's one beginner mistake you wish you had avoided in your first competitions?

I'd love to hear how different people approach the first day of a competition. I think it would help not only me but also other beginners participating in this Playground Series.

Looking forward to learning from your experiences. Good luck to everyone!

Correction to the numbers in my comment above. Three of them are wrong, and I would rather say so here than leave them for someone to copy.

The +0.0019 and +0.0027 came off a ladder whose middle step happens to carry Dariush Afshar's daily - (social + gaming + work) while the two ends do not. So the capacity row quietly absorbed his feature and the encoding row came up short by the same amount. With that feature present at all three steps, capacity is +0.0012 and the encoding is +0.0032. Same sentence, one more thing. Capacity and the encoding are two steps of one ladder, each measured on top of the last, so "each change added on its own" is only true of the feature rows.

Those were worth a tenth of the encoding here, and the encoding works for a reason that has nothing to do with smartphones: this data was generated and rounded onto a grid, and encoding the exact value picks the grid up.

A single-feature score tells you how a column ranks alone. Nothing in a model is ever alone.

title: There is no distribution shift in this data - only missingness. What that means for the private LB
content:
Following up on my earlier thread about train/test missingness rates, with the measurement I said I hadn't run yet.

I ran adversarial validation (train vs test, id excluded, 5-fold, deterministic settings) on the pooled 987,671 rows, in five variants. The question: is there real feature drift between the splits, or is it all missingness?

Variant Adversarial AUC
raw features, NaN kept, no flags 0.564146
raw + 12 is_missing flags 0.564958
is_missing flags only 0.565120
NaNs imputed away (distribution-matched) 0.503339
complete rows only 0.498486

Read the last two rows. Impute the missingness away and separability collapses to 5% of what it was. On complete rows only, the bootstrap 95% CI is [0.496194, 0.500552] - it covers 0.500, so train and test are statistically indistinguishable once you remove the NaNs.

So there is no value drift underneath. The missingness is not part of the shift; it is the whole shift.

Two consequences I think matter for the last month of this competition:

  1. The private split should behave like the public one. Whatever reshuffle happens on August 31 is unlikely to come from distribution shift, because there isn't any. That is genuinely good news and it argues against elaborate drift-correction schemes.

  2. The reshuffle risk is noise and public-split overfitting instead. I worked out what the public LB can actually resolve: for two highly-correlated submissions the smallest difference distinguishable at 95% is about 0.00015, and for weakly-correlated ones roughly 0.0013 to 0.0018. A large part of the current ordering between neighbouring teams sits inside that band. If you are selecting your final two submissions by public score, you are partly selecting on coin flips.

One correction I owe this forum. In an earlier reply I said the no-flags and with-flags adversarial AUCs were identical to six decimal places. They are not - the numbers above are the corrected ones. My first run had a bug where the flag columns were constructed but never attached to the matrix, so both arms were literally the same model. The conclusion survives but should be stated properly: dropping all twelve flags retains 98.75% of the separability, not 100%.

One thing that came out sharper on the re-run and I have not seen mentioned: 9 of the 9 numeric-column flags carry exactly zero gain - LightGBM's native NaN routing already produces that split - but the three categorical-column flags do carry gain, with academic_work_impact__isna the largest. So "drop the missingness flags" is correct for numerics and wrong-by-mechanism for categoricals.

Full run, every number computed at run time: https://www.kaggle.com/code/dariushafshar/s6e8-the-missingness-is-the-drift

Like for like my number was 0.00002 against your 0.00015, a factor of seven, not the fifteen I had written down.

Then I measured more pairs, and the seven turns out to be a property of the pair I picked rather than of your number. Once the two sds are near equal, the difference of two AUC estimates is just the variance of a difference: sd(gap) = sd(move) * sqrt(2(1 - rho)). That part is algebra, not a finding. What is measured is that it holds, within about 5% on every row below. Seven pairs from szymonkapiski's public library, 200 resamples each drawing a disjoint public-sized (59,260) and private-sized (237,042) subset of the out-of-fold training rows, sd(move) about 0.0007 throughout:

pair correlation of AUC estimates resolvable at 95%
best single vs 2nd best 0.99999 0.000005
top-8 vs top-10 0.9999 0.00002
evens vs odds of the top 20 0.9973 0.00010
top-10 vs top-20 0.9955 0.00013
top-10 vs top-40 0.9936 0.00016
top-10 vs all 74 0.9732 0.00034
best single vs 20th best 0.9543 0.00043

Your 0.00015 back-solves to a correlation of about 0.994, which lands between my top-10/top-20 and top-10/top-40 rows. So it is not a coarse number, it is a moderately correlated pair. The 0.00002 I was going to quote at you is a pair where one blend is literally a subset of the other, which is the best case available rather than a typical one.

Two things the table taught me about my own reading. Same stack does not mean high correlation: all seven pairs come from one library and they span 0.954 to 0.99999, and top-10 against all 74 resolves at 0.00034, well above the 0.0002 I was about to call decisive. What matters is how alike the two candidates are, not where they came from. And correlation of AUC estimates is not correlation of predictions: top-10 against all 74 is 0.994 on the prediction vectors and 0.973 on the AUC estimates, and it is the second that goes in the formula. If someone answers your question by correlating two submission files, the answer will come out too optimistic.

On the between-team question I have nothing, and I want to be straight about that rather than agree with you for free. Your weak band of 0.0013 to 0.0018 would need a correlation near 0.57 at my sd, far below anything I can build out of one shared library. So either real teams are much less alike than any pair available to me, or the two rulers differ: yours is a bootstrap on the actual board, mine is resampled out-of-fold training rows, which by your own result differ from test in exactly their missingness, and out-of-fold predictions across one library share a fold assignment. That shared structure inflates correlation, and correlation is the whole result. I would not bet against your number there. I just cannot reach it.

On your last paragraph, which is the part I keep coming back to. You give the mechanism for the numeric half, and I think the categorical half falls out of the same place: a missing category arrives as code -1 and gets routed to a default side rather than becoming a selectable value, so an explicit flag adds a split that native routing does not. That is my inference rather than your claim, and it is untested; a learner without native NaN handling should separate the readings. One thing worth stating alongside it: your flags-only 0.565 is an adversarial AUC, so what it establishes is that missingness carries information about which split a row came from, while the zero gain is about those flags being redundant next to the raw columns. Two different claims, and holding them apart is what makes the nine-versus-three sharp.

title: The Signal in the Noise: Treating Missing Values as Features in S6E8
content:
Hi everyone,

I've been exploring the S6E8 dataset and noticed something interesting regarding the missing values. In many real-world datasets, missing values are a nuisance to be imputed. However, in this synthetic challenge, the "missingness" itself seems to carry significant signal.

The Observation

Almost every feature in the dataset has a substantial amount of missing values. When I trained a baseline LightGBM model without handling them explicitly, the performance was decent. However, after adding binary indicators for missingness (e.g., feature_is_missing), the ROC AUC improved noticeably.

Why does this work?

In synthetic data generation, missing values are often injected based on certain rules or distributions related to the target or other features. By creating these indicators, we allow the model to learn these underlying patterns directly rather than relying on the GBDT's internal handling of NaNs.

Implementation

A simple loop to create these features:

for col in numerical_features:
    df[f'{col}_is_missing'] = df[col].isnull().astype(int)

Combined with some simple ratio features (like screen_time_ratio), this approach pushed my baseline to 0.965+ on the Public LB.

What are your thoughts? Have you found other feature engineering tricks that work well here?

Happy Kaggling!

content: In train.csv addicted_labels are binary 1 and 0 but in sample_submission file why it is something like probability. Can someone please clarify what are we actually intend to submit.

messages.text:
Always probabilities in binary competitions. Because AUC is a ranking metric, the probabilities don't even have to be on a [0, 1] scale, but it is common to submit them as such. In practical terms, that means we should use .predict_proba instead of .predict with trained classifiers.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

labels = np.array([1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0])
preds1 = np.array([0.9, 0.6, 0.8, 0.85, 0.1, 0.2])
preds2 = np.array([1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0])

roc_auc_score(labels, preds1)
roc_auc_score(labels, preds2)

In preds1 we have probabilities, and in preds2 those same probabilities converted to binary classes using 0.5 as threshold. We get a perfect AUC score of 1 in the first case and 0.833 in the second.

Hi, this is because the competition is evaluated using AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve), which measures how well your predictions are ranked by probability, not whether the classification itself is correct. So even though the labels in train.csv are 0/1, what you need to submit is the predicted probability of each row belonging to class 1 (a decimal between 0 and 1), not the predicted class itself. If you're using an sklearn model, you can get this withpredict_proba(X)[:, 1]— just make sure not to use predict(X), which returns the 0/1 class label instead.

title: The generator turned a hard rule into a smooth field: a forensic look at the synthetic layer
content:
Playground datasets are synthetically generated from a real table, which means the thing we are modelling is not the world, it is a generator's rendering of a smaller real dataset. For this episode the underlying data is known, so we can measure exactly what the generator did to it. broccoli beef posted that the original 7500 row dataset is almost a lookup table: addicted is 1 when daily_screen_time_hours is above 8 or social_media_hours is above 4, it is 0 when both are low, and a coin flip in between. I confirmed that independently, then ran the same probes on the 691k synthetic rows we are scored on. This is what the generator did.

1. It smeared the two hard rules. On the original the two rules are exact: the first region is all ones, the second all zeros, and reading them alone gives AUC 0.9888. Run the identical rules on the synthetic data and the boundaries are gone. The region that was all zeros is now 33 percent addicted, the all ones region picks up counterexamples, and the two rules together drop to AUC 0.835. The step became a slope, which is the whole difference between the two panels above.

2. It manufactured signal where there was none. In the original, the in between region is a coin flip, and a gradient boosted model on it alone scores 0.50, pure noise. In the synthetic data that same region is a third of all rows, and the same model scores 0.896 on it. The generator did not only blur the rules, it wrote real structure into what used to be noise.

3. It reshaped every marginal into a smooth curve. The clearest view is the addicted rate as a function of one feature at a time. On the original these are step functions on the two rule features and flat lines on everything else. On the synthetic data almost every feature has a smooth monotone response. The generator replaced logic with a set of soft, roughly additive effects.

4. It spread the dependence across features. On the original only two columns mattered. On the synthetic data a gradient boosted model puts real gain on several features, and the mutual information with the label is non trivial for many of them. That is why a full model beats the two rules.

5. It softened the correlation structure but kept its shape. The strongest feature correlation in the original, near 0.96, comes down to about 0.80 in the synthetic data, with the overall pattern preserved. The same pull toward smoothness shows up here too.

6. The field is calibrated and every row is unique. Out of fold predictions land on the diagonal, so the synthetic label really is a Bernoulli draw from a smooth probability field. And there are zero duplicate rows with no spike in the nearest neighbour distances, so there is no leak to exploit, only the field to fit.

What this means for modelling. The practical read is the opposite of what the original suggests. Do not hard code the two rules on this data: they cap out at AUC 0.835. A plain model on all features clears 0.95 on a sample, and that gap of about 0.12 is exactly the structure the generator added. On this competition the generator is the signal, and the job is to fit its smooth calibrated field, which is what AUC rewards.

All ten charts and every number are computed live from both datasets in the notebook, so you can fork it and check each one: https://www.kaggle.com/code/busyaprime/how-the-s6e8-generator-reshaped-the-rules

Credit to broccoli beef for the original two rule observation.

title: Train and test have different missingness rates — in all twelve columns
content:
A couple of threads here have looked at missingness — @muhammadf4h33m found is_missing flags sit at the bottom of LightGBM's gain importance, and there's been chi-square work showing missingness is independent of the target. Both match what I see. But I checked train and test separately rather than pooled, and the rates are not the same in any of the twelve columns.

Column Train % Test % Diff (pp) z
social_media_hours 19.38 16.00 -3.38 -39.8
app_opens_per_day 11.67 8.68 -3.00 -44.1
daily_screen_time_hours 13.86 11.07 -2.80 -37.9
stress_level 7.98 6.62 -1.35 -23.3
gender 4.20 4.80 +0.60 +13.3
weekend_screen_time 16.21 17.11 +0.90 +11.1
sleep_hours 6.43 7.58 +1.14 +20.7
age 4.18 5.78 +1.60 +34.6
gaming_hours 18.34 20.05 +1.71 +19.9
notifications_per_day 9.78 11.55 +1.77 +26.6
work_study_hours 7.45 9.37 +1.92 +32.2
academic_work_impact 6.40 8.68 +2.28 +40.6

Five lines to reproduce it:

import pandas as pd tr = pd.read_csv('train.csv'); te = pd.read_csv('test.csv') a = tr.drop(columns=['id','addicted_label']).isna().mean()100 b = te.drop(columns=['id']).isna().mean()100 print(pd.DataFrame({'train%': a, 'test%': b, 'diff_pp': b-a}).round(2))

At 691k and 296k rows the binomial SE of these differences is under 0.1 pp, so even the smallest gap - gender at +0.60 pp - is about 13 SEs. The direction is mixed as well: eight columns are missing more often in test, four less often. A single global deletion rate applied to both splits wouldn't produce that.

Worth being clear that this doesn't contradict the earlier findings, it's a different question. Missingness is independent of the target (I get AUC 0.50172 for a simple n_missing count, which is nothing), while the missingness rate still differs by split. Both can be true at once. Three things I think follow, stated as expectations rather than results:

  1. is_missing flags encode split identity even though they carry no target signal, so they may not transfer.
  2. Imputation statistics fitted on train are fitted to a different missingness mix than test has.
  3. An adversarial validation AUC that includes missingness flags will separate the splits for that reason alone, which shouldn't be read as feature drift.

I haven't run adversarial validation yet, so that third one is a prediction, not a measurement.

Open question for anyone further along: was the missingness injected per split independently, and does the same asymmetry show up in the candidate original dataset from the other thread?

title: Baseline Keras training, all categoricals
LightGBM Gain Importance: What the Model Actually Cares About (and What it Ignores)
content:
Hi everyone!

I’ve seen a lot of great EDA notebooks plotting beautiful distributions, but I wanted to see what the tree models actually value when making splits.

I ran a strict 5-Fold Stratified LightGBM baseline and extracted the Gain Importance (not Split Importance, which heavily biases towards continuous features). The results completely validated why my local CV wasn't improving with feature engineering.

I’ve included the full script and plots in my notebook here: https://www.kaggle.com/code/muhammadf4h33m/eda-fe-predicting-smartphone-addiction

Here is what the Gain Importance chart revealed:

1. The "Big Five" Raw Features Dominate LightGBM relies almost entirely on the raw time and dopamine-loop features to do the heavy lifting. The top 5 features by Gain are:

daily_screen_time_hours (Massive lead: ~1.8M Gain)

social_media_hours (~813k Gain)

weekend_screen_time (~786k Gain)

notifications_per_day (~314k Gain)

app_opens_per_day (~310k Gain)

2. Engineered Ratios Waste Node Splits I engineered features that looked great in EDA, like sleep_deficit (daily screen time minus sleep) and a dopamine_ratio. Because gradient boosted trees are orthogonal splitters, LightGBM was already finding the optimal boundaries using the raw features. Adding these linear combinations just diluted the feature fraction, causing my OOF ROC AUC to drop from 0.96312 to 0.96305.

3. Categoricals and Explicit NaNs are Dead Weight I tried explicitly flagging missing values in gaming_hours and social_media_hours with binary indicators. LightGBM shoved these to the absolute bottom of the importance chart alongside gender, stress_level, and academic_work_impact. The native Fisher-Weyl NaN handling already extracts the missingness signal perfectly.

The Takeaway: This synthetic dataset has such a clean, powerful raw signal that basic arithmetic feature engineering seems to act as noise rather than signal.

Has anyone found a mathematical feature transformation or grouping that actually breaks into the Top 5 for Gain Importance, or are we all just going to be hyperparameter tuning the raw data to the finish line?

title: Plot Twist: Why My "Golden" EDA Features Dropped My CV Score (EDA vs LightGBM)
content:
Hi everyone!

I spent some time digging into the continuous distributions of this synthetic dataset and found some amazing visual separations. I thought I had feature engineering in the bag, but LightGBM humbled me.

I’ve put together a comprehensive EDA notebook here: https://www.kaggle.com/code/muhammadf4h33m/eda-fe-predicting-smartphone-addiction

Here are three things I found in the EDA, and why they completely failed in cross-validation:

1. The "Silent Signal" in Missing Data (That Wasn't) social_media_hours and gaming_hours have nearly 19% missing data. I assumed this was an intentional synthetic signal (e.g., missing = 0 hours).

The Test: I created explicit binary is_missing flags.

The Reality: LightGBM assigned them near-zero Gain importance. The native Fisher-Weyl NaN handling inside the algorithm was already optimizing this perfectly. Explicit flags just added noise.

2. The "Sleep Deficit" Illusion Looking at the KDE plots, the gap between daily_screen_time_hours and sleep_hours visually splits the target classes beautifully.

The Test: I engineered a linear sleep_deficit ratio.

The Reality: The CV score dropped. Tree models are orthogonal splitters. LightGBM was already splitting screen_time > X and sleep < Y organically. Forcing a linear combination just diluted the feature fraction.

3. The 0.80 Correlation Trap daily_screen_time_hours and weekend_screen_time correlate heavily at 0.80.

The Test: I combined them into a total_weekly_screen_time feature to give the trees a cleaner split point.

The Reality: Raw daily_screen_time_hours remained the #1 most important feature by a massive margin (over 1.8M Gain), while the combined feature was largely ignored.

Takeaway: The raw signal in this synthetic dataset is already incredibly strong (my raw baseline CV is ~0.96312). Basic arithmetic combinations seem to dilute the 80% feature fraction rather than help it.

Has anyone had any luck actually improving their CV with feature engineering, or is this going to be a pure hyperparameter tuning and ensembling competition? Let me know your thoughts!

title: Handling Class Imbalance & Missing Values in This Dataset
content:
About the Dataset: Imbalance & Missing Values

This dataset has two key challenges worth discussing:

  1. Class Imbalance (Mild) The target addicted_label has a ~71/29 split:
addicted_label
1    490,474  (70.9%)
0    200,895  (29.1%)

This is a mild-to-moderate imbalance, not a severe one — the minority class still has ~200K samples, which is plenty for a model to learn from. This isn't fraud-detection-level imbalance (99:1); it's closer to a "70:30 classroom split." Since the competition metric is AUC-ROC, which evaluates ranking quality rather than raw accuracy, this level of imbalance has a fairly limited impact on scoring. Light reweighting (class_weight='balanced' or scale_pos_weight) should be enough — aggressive resampling like SMOTE probably isn't necessary here.

  1. Missing Values Almost every feature has missing values, some quite substantial:
age                         28929
daily_screen_time_hours     95854
social_media_hours         133995
gaming_hours               126821
work_study_hours            51518
sleep_hours                 44480
notifications_per_day       67584
app_opens_per_day           80710
weekend_screen_time        112063
gender                      29034
stress_level                55148
academic_work_impact        44224

social_media_hours and gaming_hours are missing in over 15-20% of rows — this is significant enough that how you handle it will likely move your leaderboard score meaningfully.

Suggested Approaches

Handling Missing Values:

Start by checking if missingness itself is informative — create binary "is_missing" flag columns for each feature before imputing. In behavioral datasets like this, missingness often isn't random (e.g., people who don't track their gaming might behave differently than those who do). For numeric features (sleep_hours, stress_level, etc.), try median or group-wise imputation (e.g., median by age bucket or gender) rather than a single global median. Tree-based models (LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost) can natively handle NaNs and often perform better than manual imputation — worth testing "leave NaN as-is" vs. imputed versions side by side. For gender (categorical), treat missing as its own category rather than imputing, since forcing a guess could introduce noise.

Handling Class Imbalance:

Since the metric is AUC, imbalance is less punishing than it would be for accuracy, but it's still worth addressing. Try scale_pos_weight (XGBoost/LightGBM) or class_weight='balanced' (sklearn) to reweight the loss instead of resampling first,because its often the simplest and most effective option. If you want to experiment further: SMOTE or other oversampling techniques on the minority class (0), or undersampling the majority class, combined with cross-validation to make sure you're not leaking synthetic samples across folds. Stratified K-Fold CV is a must here to keep the class ratio consistent across folds and get a reliable local validation score that mirrors the leaderboard.

If there were missing data points in original data, and if there was some signal in that dataset, some of it may transfer to these synthetic datasets. If no data points were missing in the original - that seems to be the case here - it is most likely that this dataset was synthesized with all the data as well. If so, it would make most sense that data points were randomly removed from it, in which case it isn't very likely that there will be a meaningful signal in missing columns. I guess it doesn't hurt to try it your way.

Until we get to at least 9:1 class ratio, I don't think there is any need to do class balancing.

The term NOMOPHOBIA is constructed on definitions described in the DSM-IV, it has been labelled as a “phobia for a particular/specific things”."

"Various psychological factors are involved when a person overuses the mobile phone, e.g., low self-esteem, extrovert personality. The burden of this problem is now increasing globally."

"Other mental disorders like, social phobia or social anxiety, and panic disorder may also precipitate NOMOPHOBIC symptoms. It is very difficult to differentiate whether the patient become NOMOPHOBIC due to mobile phone addiction or existing anxiety disorders manifest as NOMOPHOBIC symptoms."

"The signs and symptoms are observed in NOMOPHOBIA cases include- anxiety, respiratory alterations, trembling, perspiration, agitation, disorientation and tachycardia. NOMOPHOBIA may also act as a proxy to other disorders. So, we have to be very judicious regarding its diagnosis."

"Some mental disorders can precipitate NOMOPHOBIA also and vice versa. The complexity of this condition is very challenging to the patients’ family members as well as for the physicians as NOMOPHOBIA shares common clinical symptoms with other disorders. That's why NOMOPHOBIA should be diagnosed by exclusion."

"We have to stay in the real world more than virtual world. We have to re-establish the human-human interactions, face to face connections. So, we need to limit our use of mobile phones rather than banning it because we cannot escape the force of technological advancement."
